To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) younger adults' recall is facilitated by both relational and item-specific encoding, but older adults' recall is not, and (b) younger adults' free recall of categorized lists conforms to the predictions of the integrated model, but older adults do not.
the use of item-specific information is more important for older than for younger adults, and the use of relational information is less important for younger than for older adults.

1) older adults' recall is facilitated by using both rating and sorting tasks during encoding, 2) older adults' free recall is better when they encode large categories, 3) older adults' performance is not always consistent with predictions from the integrated model, 4) older adults' memory is not always better with large than with small categories, and 5) older adults' encoding and retrieval processes may be less flexible than those of younger adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of item-specific information in episodic memory.
the question of how the cognitive processes of older adults differ from those of younger adults.
the role of encoding operations in memory for words.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
older adults' memory is not as good as younger adults' but that older adults are able to compensate for their memory deficits by employing different strategies.

, for younger adults, the integrated model is a good predictor of memory performance; however, for older adults the model needs to be modified in order to account for the effects of category size and encoding task.
the effects of relational and item specific information on memory are not as simple as the integrated memory model suggests.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
older adults are not impaired in using the same information as younger adults, but that they may not be equally able to use the same information.
the effects of item-specific and relational information on memory are not independent.
the effects of relational information are more complex than previously assumed and that they may be less robust for older adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
older adults' memory is not a single, monolithic construct, but rather is a complex system that is sensitive to many different variables.
older adults' recall of items can be improved by using encoding tasks that are designed to support the integration of item-specific and relational information.
the integrated memory model can be used to understand older adults’ memory.
